description: Sampling techniques and the practical and ethical challenges shaping what sociologists can study.
content_html:
Sampling: Who to Study?

Sociologists rarely study entire populations. Instead, they select a sample from a sampling frame (a list of the target population). The goal is usually a representative sample — one that accurately reflects the characteristics of the wider population, so that findings can be generalised beyond the sample itself.

There are five main sampling methods you need to know. Random sampling gives every member of the sampling frame an equal chance of selection, minimising bias, but requires a complete list of the population. Systematic sampling selects every nth person from the list (e.g. every tenth name); practical but may introduce bias if the list has a regular pattern. Stratified sampling divides the population into groups (strata) by relevant characteristics (e.g. social class, gender, ethnicity) and selects a proportional number from each stratum, ensuring the sample mirrors the structure of the population. Quota sampling sets quotas for particular groups (e.g. 50 working-class women, 50 middle-class women) and selects participants non-randomly until quotas are filled; quick but technically not fully representative. Snowball sampling means initial participants recruit others from their social networks; useful for hard-to-reach populations but unlikely to produce a representative sample.

A sociologist wants to investigate attitudes to higher education among Year 11 students at a comprehensive school in the West Midlands. The school has 200 Year 11 students. Using a stratified sample, the researcher identifies key strata (gender, eligibility for free school meals, ethnicity) and selects a proportional number from each group. This increases representativeness: if 30% of students are eligible for free school meals, roughly 30% of the sample will be too, ensuring the findings reflect the full diversity of the year group. Snowball sampling would be inappropriate here because students are not a hard-to-reach population and the resulting sample would be biased towards existing social networks.

Practical Issues: Time, Cost and Access

Time is a fundamental constraint. A longitudinal study tracking a cohort of children from birth to adulthood might take decades — valuable, but beyond the resources of most researchers. The method must match the available timescale: participant observation is time-intensive; a self-completion questionnaire distributed online is not.

Cost constrains the scale and type of research. A large-scale national survey with a team of interviewers requires substantial funding. Academic sociologists apply to research councils; independent researchers may be limited to small local studies. Online questionnaires have reduced the cost of reaching large samples, but interviewer-led or observational methods remain expensive in labour time.

Access is often the decisive practical constraint. Some groups are hard to reach: gang members, people experiencing domestic abuse, children in care. Gatekeepers — head teachers, prison governors, social workers, community leaders — must often be persuaded before the researcher can reach participants at all. Gatekeepers can improve access but can also limit it: a head teacher who restricts research to “well-behaved” pupils introduces sampling bias by excluding the most relevant participants for a study of school exclusion.

Key Fact

The three practical issues in sociological research are time, cost and access. Access is often the most sociologically interesting: the hardest populations to reach are frequently those whose experiences are most poorly understood and most important to study.

Ethical Issues: Consent, Confidentiality and Harm

The British Sociological Association (BSA) publishes ethical guidelines that professional sociologists are expected to follow. Three ethical issues are required at GCSE: informed consent, confidentiality and harm to participants.

Informed consent means participants must be told — in plain language — what the study is about, how their data will be used, and that they can withdraw at any time without penalty. The “voluntary” element is critical: participants in a school, a workplace or a prison may feel unable to refuse even if technically told they can.

Confidentiality means that identifying information about participants must be protected: names and locations anonymised in published findings, raw data stored securely, and personal details not disclosed to employers, family members or the authorities.

Harm to participants covers a wide range of potential risks: psychological distress from discussing traumatic experiences, physical risk from studying dangerous settings, reputational damage from being identified in publications. The researcher has a duty to anticipate and minimise these risks.

Key Fact

The three ethical principles required at GCSE are informed consent, confidentiality and harm to participants. The British Sociological Association (BSA) sets guidelines requiring researchers to address all three before beginning any study.

The specification explicitly asks how ethical issues can be addressed. Students should know practical solutions, not just list the problems:

  • Informed consent: use a written consent form in plain English; for children, obtain parental consent and the child's own assent; include the right to withdraw at the start of every session.
  • Confidentiality: anonymise all names and locations in transcripts and publications; use participant codes rather than names in data files; store data on password-protected systems.
  • Harm: offer a debrief session after the research, particularly if sensitive topics were discussed; provide signposting to support services; obtain ethics committee approval before beginning.
  • Deception in covert research: covert observation necessarily involves deception, violating the BSA’s informed consent principle. Researchers must justify it by arguing that the social benefit outweighs the ethical cost, and debrief participants as soon as possible after completion.

The Tension Between Research Goals and Ethics

Ethical requirements can directly conflict with research goals. Informed consent can alter participants’ behaviour (the Hawthorne effect). Confidentiality limits what researchers can report. A sociologist wanting to study violence within criminal networks faces an almost irresolvable tension: the most valid data would come from covert observation, but gaining covert access is deceptive and could put the researcher in physical danger.

Feminist researchers studying violence against women may feel ethically obliged to empower participants rather than simply extract data — an approach sometimes called participatory research, in which participants help shape the research process. A positivist researcher, by contrast, may prioritise objectivity and distance, arguing that participant involvement would compromise validity. The ethical decisions a researcher makes often reflect their theoretical perspective.

A persistent error is to list “consent, confidentiality, harm” as three boxes to tick without reasoning about which apply to the specific research scenario and how the researcher addresses them. For a study of attitudes to school uniforms, harm is a minor concern. For a study of young people involved in serious youth violence using covert observation, harm (to participants and researcher), deception (violating informed consent), confidentiality (disclosures of criminal activity) and access (via snowball sampling) are all live and interconnected problems. The mark scheme rewards practical reasoning in context.
exam_tip_html: On a 3-mark Identify and Describe question on ethical issues, identify a specific issue (not just “ethics”) and describe both the problem and how a researcher would address it. The common error is to describe the problem at length without proposing a practical solution. For a 12-mark Evaluate on whether ethical guidelines make valuable research impossible, structure your argument around specific methods and contexts: e.g. covert participant observation of a criminal network is ethically problematic but may be the only method yielding valid data. A Mastering answer weighs the ethical cost against the research benefit and reaches a clear judgement, rather than simply listing both sides in parallel. Never treat ethical principles as a checklist — always apply them to the specific research scenario in the question.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Five sampling methods: random (equal chance), systematic (every nth), stratified (proportional by group), quota (non-random quotas) and snowball (for hard-to-reach populations). Practical constraints — time, cost and access — affect which method is feasible.
  • Three ethical principles: informed consent (voluntary agreement after full information), confidentiality (protecting identifying information), harm to participants (minimising risk). Each has practical solutions: consent forms, anonymisation, debrief sessions, ethics committee approval.
  • Ethics are not a checklist — they must be applied to the specific research context. Covert observation violates informed consent but may be justified for hard-to-access populations where the social benefit is high. The tension between research goals and ethical obligations is a real feature of sociological practice.

practice_questions.text:
Which sampling method involves initial participants recruiting others from their social networks and is best suited to studying hard-to-reach populations?
A) Stratified sample
B) Systematic sample
C) Quota sample
D) Snowball sample
Define the term 'informed consent' as used in sociological research ethics.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for indicating consent requires participants to agree to take part; 1 mark for indicating they must be given full, honest information about the study and must agree voluntarily, with the right to withdraw. Example: 'Informed consent means that participants must be given clear and honest information about the study and must voluntarily agree to take part before data collection begins.'

practice_questions.text: Identify one practical issue that sociologists face when conducting research and describe how it can affect the quality of data collected.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a practical issue (time, cost or access). Up to 2 marks for a developed description. Example: identifying access (1 mark) and explaining that if a gatekeeper (such as a school head teacher) restricts access to certain participants — for example, excluding students with poor behaviour records from a study of school exclusion — the resulting sample will be biased and unrepresentative, meaning findings cannot be generalised and the validity of the research is undermined (2 marks).

practice_questions.text: Describe two ethical issues a sociologist might face when conducting research with vulnerable participants, and explain how each can be addressed.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks for the first ethical issue: e.g. harm to participants — discussing traumatic experiences may cause psychological distress; the researcher can address this by offering a debrief session, providing signposting to relevant support services, and stopping the research if the participant shows signs of distress (1 mark for identifying harm, 1 mark for a practical solution). Up to 2 marks for the second issue: e.g. informed consent with children — children cannot legally give consent themselves; the researcher must obtain written consent from a parent or guardian and age-appropriate assent from the child, explaining the study in accessible language (1 mark for identifying the consent challenge, 1 mark for the practical solution).

practice_questions.text: Identify one ethical problem created by using covert observation as a research method and describe how a researcher might attempt to address it.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying an ethical problem specific to covert observation (e.g. deception violates informed consent; participants cannot withdraw because they do not know they are being studied; the researcher may observe illegal activity and face a legal or moral dilemma). Up to 2 marks for a developed description of how it might be addressed. Example: identifying deception (1 mark) and explaining that some researchers address this by conducting a full debrief as soon as the covert phase is complete, informing participants of the research, offering the right to withdraw data, and seeking retrospective consent — though critics argue this does not fully resolve the original deception (2 marks).

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the claim that ethical guidelines make some of the most valuable sociological research impossible to conduct.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full range of relevant arguments for both sides. Arguments in favour: some research questions (gang violence, covert institutional racism, hidden drug networks) genuinely cannot be investigated through fully consented transparent methods; the Hawthorne effect means fully transparent research produces less valid data on sensitive behaviour; historically important covert research has shaped policy in ways that fully consented research could not. Arguments against: ethical guidelines protect vulnerable participants from exploitation; the BSA guidelines provide practical solutions (anonymisation, debriefs, ethics committees) that allow sensitive research to proceed; research violating ethical principles lacks academic credibility; feminist researchers argue participant-centred approaches produce richer and more valid data than covert extraction. At least two perspectives or named methods cited. A clear supported judgement about where the balance lies.

Secure: Both sides addressed; at least one named method or context; a judgement reached.

Developing: Mostly one-sided or descriptive; some relevant points; conclusion present but not substantiated.

Emerging: Basic description of ethical issues; little evaluative engagement; no clear judgement.

knowledge_checks.q: Which ethical principle requires that participants be given full, honest information about a study and voluntarily agree to take part?
An organisation (such as a school or prison) that controls access to a research population is called a:
The ethical principle that personal information about participants must be kept private and not used to identify individuals is called '______'.
The three practical issues sociologists face in research are time, cost and '______'.
Match each ethical issue to its appropriate practical solution.
right: Provide a written consent form explaining the study and include the right to withdraw
Anonymise all names and locations in published findings and store data securely
Offer a debrief session and signpost to support services after discussing sensitive topics
Debrief participants as soon as possible and offer retrospective withdrawal of data

flashcard_questions.a: Participants must receive full, honest information about the study and voluntarily agree to take part before it begins.
Personal information provided by participants must be protected and not used to identify them in publications.
Any psychological, physical or reputational risk that the research process poses to the people being studied.
An individual or organisation that controls access to a research population and must grant permission for the study.
A sample that divides the population into strata (groups) and selects a proportional number from each.
A sample in which initial participants recruit others from their networks; used for hard-to-reach populations.

flashcard_questions.q: How can informed consent be obtained when researching children?
flashcard_questions.a: Written consent from a parent or guardian, plus age-appropriate assent from the child themselves.

flashcard_questions.q: How does covert observation violate ethical principles?
flashcard_questions.a: Participants do not know they are being studied, so cannot give informed consent or choose to withdraw.

flashcard_questions.q: What practical solution addresses harm after a sensitive interview?
flashcard_questions.a: A debrief session with signposting to relevant support services.
Replacing participants' real names and locations with codes or pseudonyms in published findings and data files.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is access a significant practical issue?
flashcard_questions.a: Gatekeepers may restrict entry and hard-to-reach groups require alternative strategies such as snowball sampling.

flashcard_questions.q: Name the professional body whose ethical guidelines UK sociologists follow.

glossary_terms.definition: A complete list of all members of the population from which a sample is drawn.
A sampling method that divides the population into groups (strata) and selects a proportional number from each, ensuring the sample mirrors the population's structure.
A sampling method in which initial participants recruit others from their social networks; used for hard-to-reach populations.
An individual or organisation that controls access to a research population and whose permission must be obtained before research can proceed.
The ethical principle that participants must receive full, honest information about a study and must voluntarily agree to take part before data collection begins.
The ethical principle that personal information provided by research participants must be kept private and not used to identify individuals.
Deliberately misleading research participants about the nature or purpose of a study; used in covert research and generally in violation of informed consent principles.

hero_image_caption: Sampling, ethical guidelines and practical constraints shape which research questions sociologists can realistically investigate.
